toc.title: The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt
Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • What makes a prompt effective: goal, context, audience, format and constraints
  • The core moves: be clear and direct, give the why, show examples, add a role, separate instructions from material
  • How to prompt for business tasks (reports, emails, plans) and technical tasks (formulas, scripts, data cleanup) without being a developer
  • How to ask Claude to ask you questions and to admit uncertainty

2The Anatomy of an Effective Prompt

Running case

Cedarbrook's Vague Request

  • A marketing coordinator types: "Write a product description for the Ridge tent."
  • Claude returns a generic, 400-word paragraph that sounds like every other tent
  • The coordinator then rewrites the request with audience, tone, length, key facts and format and gets text the team can use

Think of Claude as a brilliant new colleague who knows nothing about your company. The more precisely you explain the job, the better the result.

Element What to state Example
Goal The task and what a good result is "Write a 90-word product description that makes a family choose this tent"
Context Background, purpose, the why "It is for the spring catalog; our customers are first-time campers"
Audience Who will read it "Parents with young children; no jargon"
Format Structure, length, tone "One headline, three bullets, one closing sentence; friendly tone"
Constraints Must and must-not "Mention the 4.2 lb weight; no claims about waterproofing ratings"
Example A sample of the style you want "Here is last year's description for the Trail tent"

Key test: Show your prompt to a colleague with no background. If they would be confused about what to do, Claude will be too.

Exam tip

A weak result is most often a weak prompt, not a weak tool. The first fix is to add the missing goal, context, audience, format or constraint.

3Core Techniques

Be clear and direct

  • Say exactly what you want, including extras. If you want more than the bare minimum ("include charts and a summary"), ask for it: Claude does not guess ambitious scope from a short request.
  • Give sequential steps (numbered list) when order or completeness matters.
  • State what to do rather than only what to avoid: "write in plain sentences" works better than "don't use jargon" alone.

Give the reason

Explain why a rule exists and Claude can apply it sensibly.

Less effective More effective
"Never use ellipses." "This text is read aloud by a speech tool, so avoid ellipses, which it cannot pronounce."
"Keep it short." "Support agents read this on a phone between calls, so keep it under 60 words."

Use examples

  • Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer tone, format and structure.
  • Use three to five examples that are relevant (match the real task), diverse (cover different cases) and clearly marked as examples.
  • One example can be enough for a simple format; no example is fine for a plain task.

Separate instructions from material

  • Put pasted documents, emails or data in clearly labeled blocks (for example, tags such as <email>...</email> or lines like "Document starts / Document ends") so Claude does not confuse your instructions with the content to work on.
  • With long documents, put the documents first and the question and instructions last.

Give Claude a role

  • A single sentence such as "You are a careful financial analyst for a retail company" focuses tone and approach.
  • A role helps style and focus; it does not add knowledge Claude lacks and does not replace checking the output.

Let Claude ask and admit doubt

  • "Before you start, ask me up to three questions if anything is unclear" avoids a wrong first draft.
  • "If you are not sure, say so instead of guessing" and "quote the source line you used" reduce invented details (Module 3).

Exam tip

When a question gives two prompts and asks which will work better, pick the one with specific context, audience, format and constraints, not the shorter one and not the one that just asks for "your best work".

[Verify live] Menu names, features and model behavior change; the prompting principles above do not. Current guidance is on Anthropic's prompting best-practices page.

4Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks

Task type Prompt moves that work Cedarbrook example
Drafting (email, report, post) Name audience, tone, length; give key facts; ask for a draft you will edit "Draft a 120-word apology email to a customer whose order is 5 days late; calm, specific, offer a 10% credit"
Summarizing State the reader and the purpose; ask for key decisions and open questions "Summarize this 20-page supplier contract for the finance director: costs, deadlines, penalties"
Analysis Provide the data; define the question and the output; ask for the assumptions "From this CSV of weekly sales, which 3 categories grew fastest? Show the figures you used"
Technical help for non-developers Say your tool and your goal; paste the data shape; ask for the steps and an explanation "In Google Sheets, write a formula to total column C only where column A says 'West'; explain it in one line"
Structuring information Name the output format (table, checklist, JSON-like list) and the fields "Turn these meeting notes into a table: action, owner, due date"
  • For technical tasks you still state the goal, the tool/version and an example of the input; then test what Claude gives you on a small sample.
  • Scripts, formulas and macros that Claude writes must be tested before they touch real data or go to IT (Module 15).
Exam tip

"Business and technical tasks" does not mean building software. It means using Claude for formulas, data cleanup, templates and simple automation, and escalating real integration work to a Developer.

5Common Mistakes

Mistake Better
One-line request with no audience State the reader and purpose
Mixing five tasks in one sentence One clear task, or numbered steps (Module 2)
Pasting a document with no instructions about it Say what to do with it, and put the question after it
Assuming Claude knows your company Give facts, or put them in a Project (Module 11)
Asking "make it better" Say how: shorter, friendlier, more formal, with numbers
Treating the first answer as final Review and iterate (Module 2)

6Exam Q&A

S1A coordinator asks Claude: "Write an email about the delay." The draft is generic. What is the best next step?

  • ASwitch to a larger model
  • BAdd the audience, the reason for the delay, the tone, the length and what the reader should do next
  • CWrite the email by hand because Claude cannot do this task
  • DAsk Claude to try again with the same wording
Show the answer

Answer: B. The prompt lacks context and constraints; adding them is the most reliable improvement.

S2Which prompt is most likely to give a usable result?

  • A"Summarize this contract for the finance director in five bullets: cost, deadlines and penalties."
  • B"Give me a long and detailed summary of this whole document with as many details as possible, please."
  • C"Summarize this."
  • D"Summarize this as well as you can."
Show the answer

Answer: A. It names the reader, the format and the focus.

S3A team wants consistent product descriptions in the house style. Which technique helps most?

  • ATell Claude to be creative
  • BRemove all constraints
  • CShow two or three well-chosen examples of approved descriptions
  • DAsk for the longest possible output
Show the answer

Answer: C. Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and format.

S4A user pastes a 30-page report and then types a question in the last line. Why does this order help?

  • AClaude only reads the last line
  • BIt prevents hallucinations entirely
  • CIt lowers the cost of the request
  • DPutting the long material first and the question last improves the response to the question
Show the answer

Answer: D. For long inputs, place the documents first and the instructions or question at the end.

S5An analyst's rule says "Never use ellipses," and Claude sometimes uses them. What change is most effective?

  • AExplain the reason: the text is read aloud by a tool that cannot pronounce ellipses
  • BRepeat the rule in capital letters
  • CDelete the rule
  • DApologize to Claude
Show the answer

Answer: A. Giving the reason lets Claude apply the rule sensibly.

S6Which TWO additions make a prompt for a customer reply more effective? Select TWO.

  • AA request to answer "as fast as possible" with no other detail
  • BA sample of an approved reply
  • CThe audience and the tone to use
  • DThe word "important" at the start
  • EA statement that the task is easy
Show the answer

Answer: B, C. Audience and tone, and a good example, give Claude what it needs; urgency or praise adds no information.

S7A team lead wants Claude to avoid a wrong first draft when the brief is incomplete. Which instruction helps?

  • A"Write three different drafts at once."
  • B"Guess any missing details."
  • C"Ask me up to three clarifying questions before you start."
  • D"Do not ask anything."
Show the answer

Answer: C. Inviting questions surfaces the missing context before the draft.

S8A project manager needs a Google Sheets formula but has no coding background. What is the best approach?

  • AAsk a developer to write every spreadsheet formula for you instead of ever using Claude for this
  • BPaste the formula straight into the live sheet with real data without testing it on anything first
  • CSay nothing about the tool and hope for the best
  • DState the goal, the tool, and a sample of the data, then test the formula on a few rows
Show the answer

Answer: D. Technical help still needs clear context, and the result must be tested on a small sample.

S9Which statement about assigning Claude a role is correct?

  • AA role replaces the need to check the output
  • BA role can focus tone and approach but does not remove the need for review
  • CA role is only useful for coding tasks
  • DA role gives Claude new knowledge it did not have
Show the answer

Answer: B. Roles shape style and focus; accuracy still has to be verified.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Six elements Goal · context · audience · format · constraints · example
Key test Would a new colleague with no background understand the prompt?
Reasons Explain why a rule exists
Examples 3 to 5, relevant, diverse, labeled
Long inputs Documents first, question last; label each block
Role Focuses tone; adds no knowledge
Clarify Invite questions; ask Claude to say when unsure
Technical tasks State goal, tool, sample data; test on a small sample
